bc_neat_and_cool.blurb: A busy trad crag in the Smoke Bluffs, the small park of granite walls right beside Squamish. Climbing here is mostly cracks, corners and steep faces on granular granite, with a few bolted lines and a handful of boulder problems. Grades start around 5.6 and reach 5.13, but the bulk sit between 5.8 and 5.10, which explains the crowds. Neat and Cool (5.10a) and Flying Circus (5.10a) are the headline lines, with Cat Crack (5.7) and Kangaroo Corner (5.11a) close by. Most of the crag dries quickly after rain, though the main face stays shaded and takes longer. Bring a standard rack and expect company.

ca_middle_earth_2.blurb: Middle Earth is the southernmost of the three neighboring sectors at Mission Gorge, a granite crag inside Mission Trails Regional Park on San Diego's doorstep. The climbing is a mix of short trad lines, bolted faces and top-rope problems, with grades from 5.5 into the low 5.12s and the biggest groups at 5.10 and 5.11. Route names borrow from Tolkien: Ring My Bell (5.6) and Buttered Donkeys (5.5) are gentle, while Glamdring (5.11a) and Say My Name Sauron (5.11a) are good bolted tests. The rock is smooth and polished, so footwork matters and grades can feel stiff. It lies along the Climbers Loop, under half a mile from the visitor center lots. Start early, before the midday sun builds.
ca_middle_earth_2.parking_note: Take Mission Gorge Road to Father Junipero Serra Trail in Mission Trails Regional Park. Park along the road before the gates or in the dirt lots beside the visitor center, then walk the Climbers Loop, about 0.4 miles to the Middle Earth trailhead.

ca_main_wall_15.blurb: Main Wall is the biggest and best-known cliff at Mission Gorge, a granite crag in Mission Trails Regional Park reached by a switchbacking trail up the hillside. Routes are a mix of trad and bolted lines plus some top-rope setups, and the grades lean hard: a few 5.8s and 5.9s, then plenty of 5.10 through 5.12. The Wasp (5.11b) is a trad favorite, while Escapade (5.11a), Yellow Jacket (5.12a) and The Thumb (5.12c) are bolted. The Mission Gorge Traverse (5.8) is the long outing across the wall. The granite is polished and slick, so expect it to feel stiff for the grade. Weekends draw crowds and midday sun gets hot, so early starts are the norm.
ca_main_wall_15.parking_note: Take Mission Gorge Road to Father Junipero Serra Trail in Mission Trails Regional Park. Park along the road before the gates or in the dirt lots beside the visitor center, then follow the Climbers Loop to the second entrance, marked by a kiosk, where the trail switchbacks up to the wall.
ca_main_wall_15.approach: Leave the Climbers Loop at its second entrance, where a kiosk stands, and zigzag up the slope to the foot of the wall.

ca_6_middle_cathedral_rock.blurb: Middle Cathedral Rock is a huge granite face on the south side of Yosemite Valley, across from El Capitan, and a home of long free climbs. Almost everything is multi-pitch crack and face climbing, with most routes in the 5.10 range and a good number at 5.11 and 5.12. The East Buttress (5.10c) is the famous line, pitch after pitch of moderate cracks, and Central Pillar of Frenzy (5.9), Stoner's Highway (5.10c) and Direct North Buttress (5.10b) are other classics. Popular lines get crowded, so many parties start before first light. Decide on your descent before leaving the ground: choices include a long bolted rappel line or a scramble and short raps down the gully between Middle and Higher Cathedral.
ca_6_middle_cathedral_rock.parking_note: Use the roadside pullouts on the Valley's south side near the Cathedral Rocks. For the East Buttress, park a few hundred feet before the turnoff for El Capitan Meadow, where the climbers' trail starts at a carabiner post.
ca_6_middle_cathedral_rock.approach: Climbers' trails leave the south-side road; the East Buttress base is roughly 20 minutes up the trail. Other routes, such as those starting from the Gunsight notch, take longer and involve scrambling.

ca_mortar_rock.blurb: Mortar Rock is a small rhyolite outcrop in a Berkeley hillside neighborhood, just up Indian Rock Avenue from the larger Indian Rock. It is only about 100 feet long, yet it packs in a remarkable density of hard, technical bouldering: crimpy, powerful, often eliminate-style problems. Easier ones exist, but most of the problems are V4 and harder. Nat's Traverse (V8), Stan's Traverse (V8) and Sunshine (sit, V5) are the old standards, with harder tests like Full Fever (V10) and The Kraken (V10). Big trees keep the rock mostly shaded. It sits in a public park among homes, so park on the street, keep noise down and clean up after yourself. Getting down is a simple walk off the back.
ca_mortar_rock.parking_note: Street parking along Indian Rock Avenue, right beside the rocks. Mortar Rock is about a block uphill from the main Indian Rock.

ca_south_slope.blurb: South Slope is a hillside of granitic tonalite boulders on the sunny side of the ridge west of Lake Ramona in northern San Diego County. Nearly all of it is bouldering, with a few short trad lines mixed in. Problems run from VB to V10, with the biggest cluster between V3 and V5 and a good number at V7 and harder. Joyous (V1) and Cartwheel (V2) are the standouts at the easier end. Getting here is the real commitment: a hike of about 2.5 miles to the dam, the last mile steep, then up the hillside. With its south-facing exposure the slope gets plenty of sun, so favor cooler months and carry water.
ca_south_slope.parking_note: Park in the Blue Sky Ecological Reserve lot, which is the trailhead for the hike to the Lake Ramona dam.
ca_south_slope.approach: Hike about 2.5 miles from the parking lot to the dam, the last mile a steep grind. Once on the dam, leave the road where it first bends hard to the right and climb the slope to the boulders.

ca_happy_hunting_grounds.blurb: Happy Hunting Grounds is the best-known bouldering zone on Pine Mountain, a high forested ridge in Los Padres National Forest north of Ojai. Big sandstone boulders sit among the pines near the campground, reached by a short climbers' trail from the road, and the setting is half the appeal. Problems run from V0 up to V11, with most between V0 and V4 and a scattering of hard test pieces. Happy Hunting Grounds (V3) is the namesake, Dissing Euros (V6) and Pump Action (V4) are favorites, and Whiplash (V11) is the standout hard line. It is a long drive from Ojai on a winding road, and the elevation brings cold nights, so pack layers. Camping close by makes it a natural weekend trip.
ca_happy_hunting_grounds.parking_note: From Ojai drive north on Highway 33 to the Pine Mountain turnoff, then follow the paved road up toward the campground. Park along the road beside the boulders, and avoid parking under large trees.
ca_happy_hunting_grounds.approach: A short climbers' trail drops down from the road beside the second-to-last campsite to the boulders.

ca_mustache_wall.blurb: Mustache Wall is the first wall on the left as you enter Scheelite Canyon, a side canyon off Pine Creek Canyon above Bishop in the Eastern Sierra. The granite is steep and cracked, and the climbing is mostly bolted, with a few trad lines. It suits intermediate and advanced sport climbers: most routes are 5.11 or 5.12, with a few 5.13s, though a handful of 5.8 to 5.10 lines give warm-ups. It's Not The Wheat (5.11d), Double D ConFusion (5.11b) and The Toiler (5.12a) are good mid-range picks, while Aromatic (5.12d) and Melodramatic (5.13a) sit near the top. Bring a jacket for belaying. It sits around 7,300 feet and water is scarce, so carry plenty.
ca_mustache_wall.parking_note: From Highway 395 drive up Pine Creek Road, turn onto the dirt road opposite the campground and take the right fork to a small lot. The road is loose and rutted, especially after rain.
ca_mustache_wall.approach: Follow the track on foot into Scheelite Canyon; the first wall you pass on the left is Mustache Wall.
